subject: Kemi
title: Chemical reactions
sourceSummary: The difference between physical changes and chemical reactions, signs that a reaction has taken place, combustion and the role of oxygen, the conservation of mass, and how a simple reaction equation is read.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a chemical reaction?
questions.opener: Ask yourself whether a completely new substance is formed, or whether the substance is just changing form.
questions.explanation: When iron rusts, the iron reacts with oxygen and water, and a completely new substance is formed - rust - with different properties from the iron. Water freezing is only a physical change: the substance is still water and can melt back again.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a clear sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
questions.opener: The signs are all about something NEW having appeared.
choices: The substance has been moved to a different container
The substance got warmer because you heated it on a hotplate
A gas bubbles up or a precipitate forms, the colour changes permanently, or heat is given off by itself
The substance got wet because you poured water on it
questions.explanation: Gas being given off, a precipitate forming, a permanent colour change, or heat being released on its own all show that new substances have formed - that is chemistry. A substance getting warmer because you are heating it is not a reaction, just energy being supplied from outside.

questions.prompt: Which substance must always be present for something to be able to burn?
questions.opener: Think about why a flame goes out if you put a glass over it.
questions.explanation: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen (O₂), which is why the flame goes out when the oxygen in the glass runs out. Carbon dioxide is instead often FORMED during combustion - and it is used in fire extinguishers precisely because it displaces the oxygen.

questions.prompt: What is formed when carbon (C) burns completely in oxygen?
questions.opener: Combine the carbon with the oxygen and think about which gas plants need.
questions.explanation: Complete combustion of carbon forms carbon dioxide: C + O₂ → CO₂. Carbon monoxide (CO) is formed only during INCOMPLETE combustion, when there is not enough oxygen, and that gas is highly toxic.

questions.prompt: A magnesium ribbon with a mass of 2 g burns in air and a white powder forms that weighs more than 2 g. Which explanation is correct?
questions.opener: Something has been added from the air - what?
choices: The magnesium has reacted with oxygen from the air, and the mass of the oxygen has been added to the mass of the powder
Mass can be created out of nothing in chemical reactions
The powder became heavier because it absorbed heat
The flame that burned has a mass of its own that was left behind
questions.explanation: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, so the mass of the oxygen atoms is counted into the powder: 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO. Mass is always conserved - it is not created out of nothing, and heat has no mass that could make the powder heavier.

questions.prompt: In the reaction equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, what are the substances on the left of the arrow called?
questions.opener: The arrow means "becomes" - what comes before and after it?
questions.explanation: To the left of the arrow are the reactants (starting substances) that react, here hydrogen gas and oxygen gas. The product is what is formed and is written to the right of the arrow - in this case water.

questions.prompt: You light a wax candle. Explain what happens chemically: which substances react, what is formed, and why does the flame go out if you put a glass over the candle?
questions.opener: Start with what is burning and what it is burning together with.
questions.answer: The wax (a fuel containing carbon and hydrogen) reacts with oxygen from the air. Carbon dioxide and water vapour are formed, while heat and light are released at the same time. Under a glass the oxygen runs out and the flame then goes out, since combustion requires oxygen.
steps: Identify the fuel: the wax melts, is drawn up the wick, is vaporised and is the substance that burns. It contains carbon and hydrogen.
Identify the other starting substance: oxygen (O₂) from the air. Without oxygen there is no combustion.
Determine the products: the carbon becomes carbon dioxide (CO₂) and the hydrogen becomes water vapour (H₂O). The reaction releases energy as heat and light.
Explain the glass: the air under the glass contains a limited amount of oxygen. Once the oxygen is used up the reaction cannot continue and the flame goes out.
Check that this really is a chemical reaction: new substances have been formed and energy has been released - not just a change of form.

questions.prompt: Summarise the difference between a physical change and a chemical reaction, and what you need to know about combustion.
questions.opener: New substances or not - that is the main question. Then take combustion and mass.
questions.answer: Physical change: same substance, new form - melting, freezing, boiling, dissolving, crushing, can usually be reversed · Chemical reaction: new substances are formed with new properties - rusting, combustion, baking, digestion, hard or impossible to reverse · Signs of a reaction: gas bubbles, a precipitate, a permanent colour change, heat or light being released, a new smell · Reaction equation: reactants (starting substances) to the left of the arrow, products to the right, the arrow is read as "becomes" · Combustion: fuel + oxygen → new substances + heat and light · The fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat must all be present - remove one and the fire goes out · C + O₂ → CO₂ (carbon burns to carbon dioxide) · 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (hydrogen gas burns to water) · Incomplete combustion gives soot and toxic carbon monoxide (CO) · Conservation of mass: atoms never disappear and are never created, they only change places, so the total mass is the same before and after the reaction.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a physical change, not a chemical reaction?
questions.opener: Ask yourself whether the substance just changes form, or whether something completely new forms.
questions.explanation: When ice melts, it's still the same substance, water, just in a different form — a physical change that's easy to reverse (freeze it back). Baking, rotting and exploding all form new substances with new properties and are chemical reactions.

questions.prompt: You mix two clear liquids and a white, insoluble powder immediately forms and sinks to the bottom. What is this called?
questions.opener: The name describes something solid "falling out" of the liquid.
questions.explanation: A newly formed, insoluble substance that sinks to the bottom is called a precipitate, and it's a clear sign that a chemical reaction has taken place. A solution is instead a substance that is dissolved, not insoluble.

questions.prompt: What forms when hydrogen gas (H₂) burns completely in oxygen?
questions.opener: Combine the hydrogen with the oxygen according to the equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
questions.explanation: When hydrogen gas burns in oxygen, water forms: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide instead form when a carbon-containing fuel burns, not hydrogen gas.

questions.prompt: The ash and smoke left after a candle has finished burning together weigh as much as the candle did before, plus the oxygen that was used up. What is this principle called?
questions.opener: The principle says that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.
questions.explanation: Conservation of mass means the total mass is unchanged in a chemical reaction, since atoms only change places and form new bonds — they never disappear. That's why you have to count the oxygen from the air to make the mass add up.

questions.prompt: In the reaction equation C + O₂ → CO₂, what is the carbon dioxide that forms called?
questions.opener: It stands on the right-hand side of the arrow.
questions.explanation: What forms and stands to the right of the arrow is called a product. The carbon and oxygen to the left of the arrow are instead the reactants, the substances that react with each other.

questions.prompt: You light a gas burner with natural gas (methane). Explain what happens chemically: which substances react, what forms, and why does the flame go out if the gas supply is turned off?
questions.opener: Start with what is burning and what it's burning together with.
questions.answer: The methane (the fuel, containing carbon and hydrogen) reacts with oxygen from the air. Carbon dioxide and water vapour form, while heat and light are released. When the gas supply is turned off, there is no more fuel left, and without fuel the combustion can't continue, so the flame goes out.
steps: Identify the fuel: methane flows out of the burner and is the substance that burns. It contains carbon and hydrogen.
Identify the other starting substance: oxygen (O₂) from the air. No combustion without oxygen.
Determine the products: the carbon becomes carbon dioxide (CO₂) and the hydrogen becomes water vapour (H₂O). The reaction releases energy as heat and light.
Explain why the flame goes out: when the gas supply is turned off, there is no more fuel left to burn, and without fuel the reaction can't continue.
Check that it really is a chemical reaction: new substances have formed and energy has been released — not just a change of form.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a chemical reaction?
questions.opener: Think about which option forms a gas that wasn't there before.
choices: Water boiling and turning to steam
An effervescent tablet dissolving in water and fizzing
questions.explanation: When the effervescent tablet dissolves, carbon dioxide gas forms through a chemical reaction between the substances in the tablet, seen as bubbles — a new substance has appeared. Chocolate melting, water boiling and salt dissolving are all physical changes where the substances just change form.
